speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview of Anna Bremner was taped on June 19, 1975 by Dale Anderson at St. Mary's, Idaho. Why don't you just briefly talk about the disadvantages and advantages of rural living as you see it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think it's real good to be out where we can raise a lot of stuff ourselves and it's, we don't have a lot of neighbors around to bother us. We've got some real good neighbors. They're real nice to us. And, I don't know, I just don't think about going back to town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, talk about some of the things that you and your brothers and sisters did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we, like I said, we rode horseback, we rode, went skating, rode, went swimming. Your brothers and sisters? Yeah. Oh, yeah? Yeah, we did in high school. Yeah. Yeah. And, and at Coeur d'Alene, when we were in Coeur d'Alene, we did a lot of swimming. We were right by the lake. And, oh, I don't know. I don't know that we went on so many picnics. We went on more picnics when we were married and had children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you or your brothers or sisters expected to go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean to college? Right. No, that was, it seemed to be up to whether we wanted to go or not. My sister wanted to be a nurse, but the older one, the younger one, always wanted to. But she didn't have the help to go to be a nurse. And the other one that was, went to Idaho, the University of Idaho. She had a heart condition. But she did, hers was mostly music. She played the violin. She played the organ, played the piano. So that was most of her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she do anything with the music? No, because she... Aside from a personal thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because she didn't live long enough. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you go to business school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I suppose about a year and a half.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that the length of the curriculum or did you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it's however long it takes you to go do what you, get what you want done. You know, learn the bookkeeping and the typing and the shorthand.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were the classes structured or was it more or less paced to your individual...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To your own, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were there many people going to the school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, there was quite a few, yes. At that time, that was one of the... I think there were only two business colleges in Spokane at that time. Now I don't know that there's more. Of course now I think they go to like junior college, but there is that Kelsey Business College in Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think I've heard of another one too. Have you? I'm not even sure what the name is, but it seems like I heard that. Okay, why don't you talk about your courtship?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It started in high school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We lived over in Miltown. My folks lived in Miltown.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where's Miltown?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was way over there. It's way over there on, out of town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it's, I think, is it a mile from town, Jeff? About a mile.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does it still exist?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, the mill isn't over there. There's lots of houses over there that were built when we were there. At the time we lived in there, when my mother was over there, they had a little school there. That's where my little younger sister started school. Now there's just houses. People live over there. But I was going to say, we walked the railroad tracks all the time, going back and forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just for kicks?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's the way we, we never got out on the road.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We walked the railroad tracks.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now you wouldn't ride, you wouldn't walk a railroad track now, I don't think, because the police would go so fast, Jeff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you mean you walked down the center of the railroad track because that was a nice way to walk? Yeah. And it was clear?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, most of the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the mill was a lumber mill?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, the mill was a lumber mill. And I guess the thing was that Jim went to Palmer's school the second, and in 1912 and 13 he graduated Palmer. I graduated in 14 in St. Mary's. And I went to business college and he went to, oh, he was in the World War I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you correspond?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he wasn't a good letter writer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you a good letter writer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was a good letter writer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you write him a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not so much. Not when he was overseas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Had you talked about getting married before he went overseas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I guess so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't remember?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I think we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long was it after he came back that you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we didn't get married right away. See, he came, when did you come back? 1918?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we got married in 1920.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you working when he came back? Mm-hmm. When did you stop working?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Stopped working to, he was over in Montana. And we came over here and we got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you went back to Montana? Went back to Montana, mm-hmm. And so that was when you quit work? Yeah. Okay. What were some of your expectations before marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have a family, I think that was me. Oh, Jim didn't. Jim wanted a family too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many children did you want?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I can't say that, I just wanted a big family and I got it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many children did you have? Seven. Okay. Okay, what medical services did you have when you had your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When, from, they had a hospital in St. Mary's and all the children were born in that hospital.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where did you get your knowledge about childbirth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Dr. Cornwallet was here at the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long had he been in St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How long in St. Mary's? Yeah. Since 1911.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long was he your family doctor, or was he your family doctor?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was a family doctor, yes. But, well, he, let me see, I think I had, he lived quite a while, but I don't know what happened to him. He must have been gone someplace when Helen was born because he wasn't there, Dr. Robbins was there, he used to be the governor of the whole unit. He was there at the time that one of them was born, but otherwise Dr. Cornwallet was there all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did you keep the one doctor for most of your life here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Until he died.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you learn about child rearing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I suppose I had a book or two when I, after I got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean about raising a small child? What about just raising children in general as they got older?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just raised them. I didn't learn.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just whatever came natural? Yeah. Okay. Okay. What do you see as the future for your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they're all doing real good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever put any expectations on them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think they do what they want to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever encourage them to go to school or just once they decided you encouraged them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Now John, the other one, the boy, went to Gonzaga for two years, but then he got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever push them at home in school work or help them in any way or anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we had to help them a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that at their request or did you ever have to sit them down?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. They were pretty good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you read a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't anymore. Well, I have talking books now. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But the... Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I like to read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your children pick that up from you? Mm-hmm. What do you see in the future for your grandchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. I know that the ones in North Bend are all doing real good. And there's one, just one, no, no, there's one boy who graduated from high school last year and went to the University of Idaho. But he didn't finish his semester because he ran out of money. But then he came home and he went to work at the plywood. He says he's going back. And the other grandchildren seem to be getting married. We had five weddings last year, grandchildren married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you get together many of the weddings?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went to, we were all but one. One was in San, the oldest boy that was in North Bend, that's in Rhode Island now, was married in San Diego and was in the Navy. We went to that one and we went to, and his sister got married in August and we went to that one. And there was, two got married here and one got married in Klamath Falls. We didn't go to that one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many grandchildren do you have? Seventeen. And great-grandchildren? Four. Okay. Do you ever kind of look into the future and see what life might be like in the future for your great-grandchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any thoughts about how lifestyles have changed? Or how your lifestyle has changed?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't think my lifestyle has changed so much. Because we're, I've longed, you know, like the grandmothers have come, but we don't go very much, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you travel, what about your travels? Early life and then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not too much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about vacations?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we don't take a vacation. Oh, we didn't take one this year. We did go, we have been going over to North Bend every year. But, and we went to San Diego for that wedding. But, you know, to Coeur d'Alene, Jim and his sister are down there. That's about as far as we go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your vacations since you've been married, are those to see relatives or those for your enjoyment?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly to see relatives. Well, that's good to know. We enjoy that kind of a vacation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Visiting relatives? You have a close family? That's really nice. Do you usually just kind of set aside time? No. During the year, like a week or just?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we have to, we usually do, we've been going to, we were going over to North Bend in the fall, you know, after all the garden was all. But the last year, the year before we went in the spring, you know, before the fort was done, put the garden in. We had a, Jim and his sister, that we went to California to, I believe we went, did we go two or three times? To visit her. She lived in Oakland. And we enjoyed that. She was, she was a widow. And she took us around lots of places, just lots, we saw a lot of places. And we went down to see her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you enjoy doing that type of traveling? Mm-hmm. What states have you been in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not many.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years were you in Wisconsin?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, until I was about 13.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you moved?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I never been back there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Really? No. Do you have any family in Wisconsin?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No, they're gone, they're moved away from us. My mother had a sister that lived, not in River Lake, but she had in Medford, Wisconsin, and, but she's gone. And I think all her family, I don't think any of her family was there, is left there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about your husband's family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We haven't got many left. We just got, we just had his sister, Carlene, and himself left of the family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anyone in Michigan, or just everyone? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Idaho? In Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've been to California, and Oregon, and Washington, and Idaho? In Idaho. And you came by train out here? Yeah. How did you travel to the other states?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we flew to California. Once we went, the first time I think we went down on the bus. We'd go to North Bend and stop there, and then we went down. Then we went down on the bus, but the other time we flew down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you rather ride the bus or fly?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't like the bus. The only thing about, I think about riding a bus, you see more scenery than flying, but you, but when we went to that wedding, our daughter and her husband and one of their boys, we went with them, and that was the mother and father of the boy that was getting married. We went, we drove. That was nice, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you, what mode of travel do you like the best? Plane, train?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I'd like to get on a train again, but I haven't been on one since. Oh, when we first came to St. Mary's, there was passengers running through St. Mary's. The only time we'd get to Spokane would be on a passenger.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years did you have that service?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't remember how long that service was taking. And then another thing, when we were, when we were, when we first, when we came to St. Mary's, we came up to St. Mary's on a boat, the big boats, you know, that came up to St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: From Coeur d'Alene?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: From Coeur d'Alene.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Down the river, or up the river.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's up the river. There's, where did you get that book?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The way it was. What kind of boat is it? Was it just a steamboat? Uh-huh. With a paddle wheel? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Jim, why don't you get that book? The way it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you like about riding the train?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I liked it. I liked the train. I think maybe because I'd like to ride it again, and they don't have them, you know. I mean, they, like, when the trains used to go through St. Mary's, the passengers, and... We went to... Yeah, we went to Seattle. I went to Seattle on the train. We went to Seattle on a train for the Seattle Fair.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go to the Space Needle?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Jim did, but I was, we went to some restaurant, and I got sick from what I had to eat there. Now, it's down the bottom ones, Jim.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go to the fair in Spokane?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which one did you like the best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Spokane was a lot better than Seattle. Really? Oh, my, I should say. And, you know, our daughter had come from North Bend, and they'd heard that the fair was no good over here. And our daughter, the daughter that lives here, took them to the fair, and they spent a whole day, and they just thought it was wonderful. It must be under something, Jim, under a piece, under a tablecloth or something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you like about the Spokane Fair over the Seattle Fair?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there was more to see and more to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My husband liked the Seattle Fair better than the Spokane Fair. And that was the only one I've ever seen, so I can say. Have you ever been to any other world fairs? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you better quit looking for it, Jim. It's not in either of the two top drawers, I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you see more countryside in a train versus a bus, or is it about the same?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I imagine it's about the same. About the same. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do now for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we don't do much. We don't, uh, we just go to the meetings of the organizations that we belong to, and that's about all we do. Once in a while we take a ride up the river. And not on the boat, but we go for a ride and pick up now, because I don't have a car. But it's easier to drive or pick up somebody if you can't drive. And you're sitting up higher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you get together with your family. On holidays mostly? Holidays, birthdays.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We go up there. We've been up to. Oh, sure. Look at the boat. Find the boat for her. Oh, that's good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Turn the page there. Oh, and a log cabin. Like this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can't see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's, uh, the Georgie Oaks.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, that's the Georgie Oaks. And there was one called the Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which one were you on?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, there were the Flyer and the Georgie Oaks and the Idaho and the Flyer were the ones that came. They came up from Carlene every day at that time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh. All those boats ran the river?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, just one. They were on the river, but they. There was always that big boat that came up to St. Mary that. And they had a lot of passengers, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far down the river did it go? Carlene. From Cordelane to St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did it go up St. Joe? Yeah. Up St. Joe. But St. Joe, there's no town there now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's interesting. I want to look at that some more. Okay, why don't you describe what you've done around your house?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Around my house?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. The type of work that you do, your day-to-day life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I used to do a lot of embroidery work, you know, a lot of crocheting and sewing and stuff like that, but I don't do that anymore. It's just, oh, just ordinary work. It takes me till noontime. We have our dinner at noontime, and it takes me most of the morning to get everything done for dinner, you know, like make a pie. I make bread twice. I make bread every week. I make two loaves and put one loaf in the freezer, and two loaves last a week. Sometimes I have to get a little ahead of that. And I make a lot of cookies. And I write letters. I have a tape recorder and a cassette. That's what I use a lot for letters now. My typing is going down again. So you mail those off? Because I can't see it, huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you correspond with old friends, or is it mostly family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly family. Mostly family, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about the friends that you had when you were in high school? Are they still in town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there's one. There's just about, oh, there's a few here, but the one, there's one friend, but she's a businesswoman. She has the credit bureau in St. Mary's, and she's working. She's still working.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that Gribner?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's Margie Smith, but we put that on our name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. I was going to say, I remember you put the name down.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, Margie Smith, that's her. There's a few. Mrs. Scribner is a good friend of mine, but I didn't know her long, like in school. She wasn't here at that time. She came here after she got married. Well, there's a few that I knew, you know, the older people. Well, the church has just changed so much. I mean, there's so many new people here. This plywood people brought plywood, and now the railroad came in. There's just so many new people. We don't even know. We're strangers in church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you feel about all the new people coming into the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's good for the town because I don't think there's so much unemployment in St. Mary's. There's lots of places.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you describe the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I love the town, the whole town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does everybody feel that way about St. Mary's? I think they do. They do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they do. There was one couple that was sitting next to us, and they got up and left. I don't know. They had something to do. They come from California two or three years ago, and they just think St. Mary's is the most friendly town that they ever saw. They lived in lots of places in California, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before the new industries and the new people came in, was St. Mary's a pretty stable town? I mean, were the people who—most of the people had lived here a long time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A long time, yes, a long time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it just recently that you've had a lot of new people come in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, after the plywood came in, there have been a lot of new people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know if those people find St. Mary's a friendly town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think they do. A lot of them. I don't know whether everybody does, because we don't belong to a lot where we go like the Elks or the Eagles, where we're around and mixed with people like that. I think a lot of people think St. Mary's is a really nice place. There's a lot they can do to St. Mary's, like the streets and things like that, but we didn't want to leave. None of our children want to leave, the oldest girl. She was over in Seattle going to nurses' training when she met her husband. He was in the Navy. But they have talked lots of times of coming back to St. Mary's when they retire. They still have two boys. They had one boy graduate from high school this year, and they still have two boys. As long as those boys have children in school, I don't think they'll come, because they have that junior college over there, and the boys are the whole family of good workers, and they're known to be good workers.
